speaker: John Schulman
title: John Schulman (OpenAI Cofounder) — Reasoning, RLHF, & plan for 2027 AGI
question: Compared to fields like the social sciences that suffer from replication crises, why does machine learning research stay relatively self-correcting despite flawed academic incentives?
guest: Everyone has their complaints about the ML literature, but overall I think it's a relatively healthy field compared to some other ones, like in the social sciences, because it's largely grounded in practicality and getting things to work. If you publish something that can't be replicated easily, then people will just forget about it. It's accepted that often you don't just report someone's number from their paper—you also try to implement their method and compare it to your method on the same training dataset. So if you publish methods that are really hard to implement or really finicky, they tend to get forgotten, and as a result people actually try to open source their work a lot. There are various unfavorable incentives—people are incentivized to make the baseline methods they're comparing to worse, and there are mild pathologies like trying to make your method seem sophisticated mathematically. Overall, I feel like the field makes progress, though I'd like to see more science and trying to understand things rather than benchmark hill climbing.

points.core: Practical utility filters out brittle ML methods that fail to replicate.
points.note: Accept: grounding in getting real systems to work means irreproducible, finicky, or hard-to-implement papers get ignored and forgotten. Do not credit: claiming peer review catches all bad papers.

points.note: Accept: researchers re-running baselines on the same dataset rather than trusting paper numbers incentivizes authors to release working open-source implementations. Do not credit: generic praise for open science without linking it to re-implementation norms.

points.core: Publication incentives still push researchers to under-tune competing baseline methods.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Machine learning stays relatively self-correcting mainly because replication is cheap, fast, and built into how the field actually works. In the social sciences, checking a result often means recruiting new participants and running a costly study over months, so few results ever get retested. In ML, code, data, and model weights are usually public, and rerunning an experiment can take hours or days. More importantly, people don't replicate out of duty; they replicate because they want to build on the work. A method that genuinely helps gets adopted, tested on new problems, and folded into practical systems, while one that doesn't hold up quietly gets abandoned when others can't make it work.

Shared benchmarks, public leaderboards, and strong industry involvement reinforce this: there is a real-world test of whether something works, with money riding on it, independent of what a paper claims.

The correction is imperfect, though. Published papers still contain overstated gains from weak baselines, tuning disparities, benchmark overfitting, and data leakage, and those papers are rarely retracted. The field corrects by ignoring what fails rather than by fixing the record.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Machine learning shares academia’s flawed incentives, including publication bias, hype, and benchmark overfitting, yet remains relatively self-correcting because verification is cheap, fast, and tied to practical utility. Unlike social science studies, which often require costly, months-long human-subject data collection under shifting real-world conditions, machine learning experiments run in software on shared datasets. Strong norms around preprints, open-source code, and public model weights let peers reproduce and stress-test new claims within days rather than years.

More decisively, the field faces immediate engineering and commercial selection pressure. Competing researchers and industry practitioners constantly adopt published techniques as building blocks for larger models, fresh benchmarks, and production systems. Methods whose reported gains stem from cherry-picked seeds, fragile hyperparameter tuning, or benchmark leakage quickly fail to generalize or scale outside the authors’ original setup. Even without formal retractions, brittle ideas are rapidly filtered out through practical disuse, while genuinely robust advances survive because downstream systems measurably work better with them.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Machine learning corrects itself faster mainly because its claims are cheap to test and costly to fake. A social-science finding usually rests on one expensive study of human subjects that may take years to repeat. An ML result is mostly software. When authors release their code, data and model weights, other people can rerun the work in hours or days. Results are reported against shared public benchmarks, so a method that doesn't really help shows up quickly when others try to build on it.

The strongest check, though, is practical use. Industry labs and open-source developers adopt techniques that actually make products better and quietly drop the ones that don't, whatever the citation counts say. Methods that last, like attention, batch normalization and Adam, earn their place because they keep working across many tasks. Fast publishing through arXiv and conferences also lets corrections spread quickly.

Still, "relatively" matters here. ML has real reproducibility problems: overfitting to benchmarks, data leakage (documented by Kapoor and Narayanan across hundreds of papers), weak baselines, hyperparameter tuning that isn't disclosed, and huge models that only a few labs can afford to retrain. Those last results are as hard to check as a social-science study.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Machine learning stays relatively self-correcting because its claims face fast, low-cost, and practical verification. Unlike the social sciences, where replicating a study can require months of recruiting participants and navigating noisy human contexts, ML relies heavily on open code, shared datasets, and public benchmarks. When a paper introduces a new architecture or training method, other researchers can test it within days and immediately try building on top of it.

Equally important is intense engineering selection pressure outside academia. Companies and open-source communities adopt techniques only when they deliver reliable gains at scale and on new data. If an academic result depends on fragile hyperparameter tuning, weak baselines, or benchmark overfitting, practitioners quickly see it fail in the wild and abandon it. Although hype and flawed evaluation still occur, the tight feedback loop between published ideas, open implementations, and real-world utility steadily filters out methods that do not genuinely work.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Machine learning is relatively self-correcting because many of its claims are cheap to retest and matter to people who want to build on them. When a paper claims that a method improves accuracy or cuts training costs, other teams often have the code, data, and metrics to check. They have a practical reason to do so: they want to know which method to use or which baseline they need to beat. An overstated result can lose influence through routine follow-up work, even if nobody publishes a formal replication.

In many social-science studies, checking a claim can require recruiting new participants, recreating an intervention, or collecting years of data. A failed replication can also be harder to interpret when the population or setting differs. Machine learning’s advantage is strongest where evaluation is cheap and independent. It weakens when teams tune repeatedly on the same benchmarks, rely on private data, or need compute that few others can afford.

points.why: Researchers retest claims to decide what to use, and results that fail those checks can lose influence.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Machine learning has a relatively fast feedback loop. When a paper claims that a method improves prediction, other researchers can often run the code, compare it with a strong baseline on held-out data, and see whether the gain survives. They also have a practical incentive to check. If their own system depends on the claimed improvement, testing it advances their work even when publishing a replication earns little credit. In some social sciences, an equivalent check requires recruiting a new sample and recreating the conditions of the original study, which can take much longer.

That advantage is strongest for measurable performance claims. A model can repeatedly win on a benchmark because of data leakage, and a real performance gain can come with a mistaken explanation. Machine learning tends to correct fastest when people independently test a result under the conditions where they need it to work.
